$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit
hyperboloid.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). Write the transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr),\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr),\qquad x'^2=x^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|<c$, and $\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. Then the coordinate velocity $w'$ of $y$ in the chart $x'$ is given by $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, the denominators being positive; moreover $|w'|<c$, and $|w'|=c$ exactly when $|w|=c$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let
$x:I\to A$ be a curve whose coordinate representation in an inertial chart is
of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]) with
everywhere future timelike coordinate derivative. An **ideal clock** carried
along $x$ reads, between parameters $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

There is no additional acceleration-dependent term in the reading: the reading
depends only on the curve and the interval, not on the acceleration
(**clock hypothesis**). The integrand is a positive continuous function of $s$
on the compact interval $[a,b]$, so the integral is a well-defined Riemann
integral.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are exactly the future
null straight lines

$$\{\,p+\lambda v:\lambda\in\mathbb R\,\},\qquad p\in A,\quad v\in V\ \text{future null},$$

parametrized at $p$ by $\lambda=0$. In every inertial chart $x$, such a ray has

$$x(\lambda)=x(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3),$$

and because $v$ is future null the components satisfy $v^0=\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert>0$
by the orthonormal-coordinate description of the closed cones
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]): hence the spatial coordinate
velocity of the ray has magnitude $\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert/v^0\cdot c=c$ in
**every** inertial chart, with $x^0=ct$. The adopted conversion constant $c$ is
therefore the same in all inertial charts; its numerical value is an empirical
parameter of the model.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt the assumption that the equations of the specific mechanical and
electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the
inertial changes of description: each such model equation has the same form
when its events are relabelled by $F$ and its displacements and other tensors
are transformed by $L$.

derivations.claim: Setup: the boost transition is $x'^0=\gamma\bigl(x^0-\tfrac{v}{c}x^1\bigr)$, $x'^1=\gamma\bigl(x^1-\tfrac{v}{c}x^0\bigr)$, $x'^2=x^2$, $x'^3=x^3$, and the inverse relation is the boost of parameter $-v$; the worldline $y$ of [F1](i) is a future timelike worldline carrying an ideal clock, and its coordinate time in $x$ is $t=\lambda/c$ by the SI convention $x^0=ct$ ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], [F1], [F2], [F6]).

Clause (i): by [F1](i) the proper time of $y$ between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$, and by [F2] the ideal clock carried along $y$ reads exactly this proper time; since $t$ runs from $\lambda_0/c$ to $\lambda_1/c$, the reading is $(t_1-t_0)/\gamma$. Writing $\Delta\tau:=(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$ for the clock's reading and $\Delta t:=t_1-t_0=\gamma\Delta\tau$, we obtain $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$. A clock at rest in $x$ is at rest in the primed frame at velocity $-v$, and the same computation applied to the inverse boost of parameter $-v$ gives the symmetric statement, so the factor is the same in both directions.

Clause (ii): let the rod at rest in $x'$ have endpoints on the worldlines $y_a,y_b$ of [F1](ii), whose $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$. At a fixed $x$-time the endpoints are two events with equal $x^0$ and $x$-separation $L_0/\gamma$ by [F1](ii); they lie in the simultaneity slice of $x$ through their midpoint in the sense of [F4], and their rest distance in that slice is the Euclidean norm of their spatial coordinate difference, namely $L_0/\gamma$. Since the measurement protocol of clause (ii) assigns to the rod exactly the rest distance between the endpoint events at equal measuring-frame time, the length assigned by $x$ is $L_0/\gamma$. Exchanging the roles of $x$ and $x'$ in [F1](ii) and repeating the argument gives the symmetric statement; the rod is modelled by two straight worldlines at rest in the measuring frame's complement, so the computation applies only to a rod in uniform motion and never to a rod whose state of motion changes.

Clause (iii): by [F1](iii), events with equal $x^0$ and first-coordinate separation $L$ have $x'^0$-difference $-\gamma\tfrac{v}{c}L$, which is nonzero exactly when $vL\ne0$, so the two events are not simultaneous in $x'$; this exhibits the observer dependence of simultaneity. Chart simultaneity is equality of $x^0$, which by [F4] is exactly the slice relation $H(m,e_0)$ of the frame's time axis; and by [F3] the radar protocol of the inertial observer reproduces $x^0/c$ and the chart distance on events with nonzero spatial coordinates, so these simultaneity slices have the stated operational content.

Clause (iv): apply [F1](iv) to the worldline of the clause, which is $C^1$ future timelike with subluminal coordinate velocity $w$ in $x$; this gives the displayed transformation and $|w'|<c$ whenever $|w|<c$. For the identification of $w'$ as a relative velocity, [F5] with $n=e'_0$ and $u=U/c$ gives $w_{\mathrm{rel}}=c\,h'(U/c)/(-\eta(e'_0,U/c))$, and clause (e) of [F5] states that for the chart of the frame this coincides with the coordinate velocity in that chart, namely $w'$. Finally, the deviation from the Galilean sum is exact: $w'_1-(w_1-v)=\frac{(vw_1/c^2)(w_1-v)}{1-vw_1/c^2}$ by a single algebraic simplification of the displayed formula, so the transformation coincides with the difference $w_1-v$ exactly when $v=0$ or $w_1=0$ or $w_1=v$, and not in general.

Conclusion and scope: steps 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 and 1.5 establish clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) as statements about the ideal model, each derived from the mathematical content of [F1] together with the adopted ideal-clock reading [F2], the radar identification [F3] and the observer-relative velocity identification [F5]; the symmetric halves of (i) and (ii) use the inverse boost as in [F6]. Clause (v) records the honest qualification: the deduction is conditional on the adopted postulates and stated protocols, it produces no measurement outcome, no statistical inference and no empirical comparison, it says nothing about real clocks, rods, optical appearance, accelerating or deformable bodies, gravity or quantum effects, and it does not establish the exclusive truth of the model; the assignments are intrinsic to the measuring frame and its simultaneity slice.

boundaries.evidence: The theorem concerns two given inertial frames and displayed data; no empty family is quantified over, and clause (v) states the scope. This disposition is part of the statement.

Zero cases are separated: $v=0$ gives $\gamma=1$, the clock and rod formulas reduce to equality of rates and lengths, and the simultaneity shift vanishes; step 1.5 records the exact conditions under which the velocity formula reduces to the Galilean difference.

Clause (i) applies to a single clock worldline and clause (ii) to a rod with two endpoint worldlines; the transverse velocity is the single perpendicular component. This disposition is part of the statement.

Clause (ii) states that no claim is made about a rod whose state of motion changes, and clause (v) excludes accelerating or deformable bodies; the transformation denominators $1-vw_1/c^2$ are positive (step 1.5).

Clause (i) uses strict parameter values $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$, and clause (iv) assumes the open subluminal condition $|w|<c$; the boundary $|w|=c$ is excluded by hypothesis. This disposition is part of the statement.
The frames, boost parameter and worldlines are given data, and each reading is a conditional deduction from the named postulates; no choice principle is used in the deduction (step 2.1).
Step 1.2 derives the forward physical reading $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ from the proper-time formula, and step 1.5 derives $|w|<c\Rightarrow|w'|<c$.
Step 1.5 uses the exact identity $w'_1-(w_1-v)=(vw_1/c^2)(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ to characterize precisely when the Galilean difference is recovered, the reverse reading of the transformation.

**(a) Preservation.** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline and let $X,Y:I\to V$ be $C^1$ Fermi–Walker transported fields along $x$ ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]]). Then $\tau\mapsto\eta(X(\tau),Y(\tau))$ is constant on $I$; in particular Fermi–Walker transport preserves norms and orthogonality, and the unique Fermi–Walker transported family with initial values a tetrad $(E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0))$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ is an orthonormal tetrad $(E_0(\tau),\dots,E_3(\tau))$ at every $\tau$ with $E_0(\tau)=U(\tau)/c$ (observer-adapted tetrad), by [[lem-sr-fermi-walker-transport-existence-and-uniqueness]].

**(b) Rindler wedge congruence.** In an inertial chart $(x^0,x,y,z)$ consider $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z):=(\rho\sinh\theta,\rho\cosh\theta,y,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$, with $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\rho>0$. Then $\Phi$ is a smooth bijection onto the right wedge $W:=\{(x^0,x):x>|x^0|\}$, with smooth inverse $\rho=\sqrt{x^2-(x^0)^2}$, $\theta=\tfrac12\log\bigl((x+x^0)/(x-x^0)\bigr)$ ([[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]], [[def-hyperbolic-functions]]); the pullback of $\eta$ is $g=-\rho^2d\theta^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$; the field $n:=\rho^{-1}\partial/\partial\theta$ is a future unit timelike field on $W$ whose congruence is Born rigid and irrotational, with acceleration $a=\nabla_nn=\rho^{-1}\partial/\partial\rho$, hence $\eta(a,a)=\rho^{-2}$; its rest slices $\theta=const$ are hyperplanes orthogonal to $n$ with induced metric $d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$ independent of $\theta$; and the frame $(n,\partial/\partial\rho,\partial/\partial y,\partial/\partial z)$ is a tetrad field which is not a coordinate frame, since $[n,\partial/\partial\rho]=+(1/\rho)n$ is nonzero ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]).

**(c) Rigid rotation, ambient nonintegrability and ring holonomy.** Fix real $\Omega$. In the inertial chart let $U_\Omega$ be the open timelike region $r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2<c^2/\Omega^2$ when $\Omega\ne0$, and the whole chart when $\Omega=0$. On this four-dimensional open set put $K=\partial_0+(\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1+x^1\partial_2)$, $\gamma(r)=(1-\Omega^2r^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and $n=\gamma(r)K$. This is a smooth future unit timelike Born-rigid congruence. If $\Omega\ne0$, its three-dimensional rest distribution in the ambient open set is nowhere integrable: its vorticity is nowhere zero and no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists locally. If $\Omega=0$, $n=\partial_0$ is inertial and irrotational, and the rest hypersurfaces are $x^0=const$. Now fix $R>0$ with $|\Omega|R<c$ and restrict to the timelike ring cylinder $r=R$, $x^3=const$, whose rotating angle is $\varphi=\phi-\Omega t$ modulo $2\pi$, with $x^0=ct$. The ring observer $\phi=\phi_0+\Omega t$ has $n=\gamma(R)\bigl(1,-(\Omega R/c)\sin\phi,(\Omega R/c)\cos\phi,0\bigr)$. The induced metric is $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt^2+2\Omega R^2\,dt\,d\varphi+R^2d\varphi^2$. The ambient rest covector restricted to the cylinder is proportional to $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt+\Omega R^2d\varphi$, so the one-dimensional rest distribution on that cylinder is locally integrable and satisfies $dt/d\varphi=\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)$. After one positive circuit in the rotating label, its lift starting at $t=0$ has signed time offset $\Delta t=2\pi\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)$. For $\Omega\ne0$ it returns to the same rotating label at a different time and does not close as a ring rest-simultaneity curve; there is no globally single-valued real rest-synchronization time on the entire cylinder with time-oriented nonzero differential annihilating these rest lines. This global ring holonomy is distinct from the ambient local Frobenius obstruction. For $\Omega=0$ the offset is zero and ring rest lines are $t=const$.

**(d) Bell first-order field.** Let $q:J\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$ with $q(t)=(q_1(t),0,0)$ and $|q_1'(t)|<c$, and consider the $C^1$ future unit field of the translated worldlines $x_\xi(t)=(ct,q(t)+\xi)$ parametrized by $\xi$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, with $n=\gamma\bigl(1,q_1'(t)/c,0,0\bigr)$, $\gamma=(1-q_1'(t)^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and unit longitudinal rest vector $s=\gamma\bigl(q_1'(t)/c,1,0,0\bigr)$. For this $C^1$ field define the first-order rest projection $h^a{}_b=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b$ and projected deformation $\theta_{ab}=h^c{}_ah^d{}_b\partial_{(c}n_{d)}$, using the explicit first-order version of [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]. These coordinate formulas need only $C^1$ $n$, give a continuous tensor, and agree with the smooth congruence definitions when $q$ is smooth; in this first-order sense Born rigidity means $\theta=0$. Then

$$\theta(s,s)=s^as^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3q_1'(t)q_1''(t)/c^3,$$

which is nonzero exactly when $q_1'(t)q_1''(t)$ is nonzero; hence the congruence is not Born rigid on any neighbourhood of a parameter value with $q_1'(t)q_1''(t)\ne0$, although for every fixed chart time $t$ the separation between the members labelled $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ is the constant $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$. A breaking or fracture conclusion about a material rod would additionally require an elasticity model and a failure criterion and is not a kinematic statement.

Let $n$ be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\nabla$ be the flat covariant derivative of the affine model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), and write $n_b:=\eta_{bc}n^c$ for the associated covector field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

**(a) Rest metric and projection.** Define $h(v,w):=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)$ for vectors at the same point, so that $h=\eta+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ in components. Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). At every point $h$ is symmetric with radical spanned by $n(p)$, and its restriction to $n(p)^\perp$ is positive definite ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(c) Kinematic decomposition.** Set $\theta_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}$ and $\omega_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}$, where $\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d+\nabla_dn_c)$ and $\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d-\nabla_dn_c)$. Then

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $\theta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar**, its trace-free part is the **shear**, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**.

**(d) Born rigidity.** The congruence is **Born rigid** (it describes a rigid motion) when $\mathcal L_nh=0$. Since $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=2\theta_{ab}$, Born rigidity is equivalent to $\theta=0$, equivalently to the projected symmetrized derivative of $n^\flat$ vanishing.

**(e) Scope.** These are kinematic definitions for a prescribed smooth field $n$ on the affine model; no dynamical equation, matter model, global synchronization or completeness is assumed, and $a$, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $h$ are local objects on $\Omega$.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Flow box.** If $X$ is a smooth vector field on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]) and $X(p)\ne0$ at a point $p\in\Omega$, then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in $\Omega$ and a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^0$; the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are therefore the $u^0$-coordinate lines up to reparametrization. In particular every observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) admits a local $n$-adapted chart, and in such a chart $n=\partial/\partial u^0$.

**(ii) Frobenius criterion.** For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]) let $D:=\ker\alpha$ be the hyperplane distribution $D_p=\{v\in V:\alpha_p(v)=0\}$. Then $D$ is integrable on $\Omega$ (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding $D_p$) if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

**(iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences.** Let $n$ be an observer congruence on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\alpha:=n^\flat$, and let $\theta,\omega$ be its expansion and vorticity ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]). Then:

(a) $d\alpha=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$, that is, $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn^\flat)(Y)-(\nabla_Yn^\flat)(X)$ for smooth vector fields $X,Y$;

(b) for every $p$ and all $X,Y$ with $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ one has $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$; consequently $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(p)=0$ if and only if $\omega(p)=0$, and on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ the following are equivalent: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$, $\omega=0$ on $U$, and the rest distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$;

(c) when the rest distribution is integrable on $U$, its integral hypersurfaces are orthogonal to $n$ at every point and the restriction of $\eta$ to each of them is positive definite, so they are rest slices of the congruence.

**(iv) Scope.** All statements are local on $\Omega$; no global foliation, global synchronization, completeness or product structure is asserted, and no claim is made about variable-rank or non-smooth distributions.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

derivations.claim: Numerical data: $\Omega R=3c/5$ gives $\Omega^2R^2=9c^2/25$, hence $c^2-\Omega^2R^2=16c^2/25$, $2\Omega R^2=2(\Omega R)R=6cR/5$, $\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)=(3cR/5)/(16c^2/25)=15R/(16c)$ and $\gamma(R)=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$; the ring field is $n=\gamma(R)\bigl(1,-(3/5)\sin\phi,(3/5)\cos\phi,0\bigr)=\frac54\bigl(1,-\frac35\sin\phi,\frac35\cos\phi,0\bigr)$.

Future unit property: by [L3], $\eta(n,n)=\frac{25}{16}\bigl(-1+\frac{9}{25}(\sin^2\phi+\cos^2\phi)\bigr)=\frac{25}{16}\bigl(-1+\frac{9}{25}\bigr)=-\frac{25}{16}\cdot\frac{16}{25}=-1$, and the time component $\frac54>0$ makes $n$ future; this verifies the formula of the Example.

Cylinder metric and rest covector: substituting $\phi=\varphi+\Omega t$, hence $d\phi=d\varphi+\Omega\,dt$, into $-c^2dt^2+R^2d\phi^2$ (the transverse coordinates being fixed) gives $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt^2+2\Omega R^2dtd\varphi+R^2d\varphi^2$; with the values of step 1.1 this is $-\frac{16}{25}c^2dt^2+\frac65cR\,dtd\varphi+R^2d\varphi^2$. The covector $\kappa$ of [L1] restricts as $-c\,dt+(\Omega R^2/c)d\phi=-c\,dt+(\Omega R^2/c)(d\varphi+\Omega dt)=-\frac{c^2-\Omega^2R^2}{c}dt+\frac{\Omega R^2}{c}d\varphi$, so $n^\flat=\gamma(R)\kappa$ is proportional to $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt+\Omega R^2d\varphi=-\frac{16}{25}c^2dt+\frac35cR\,d\varphi$; solving the kernel condition $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)\dot t+\Omega R^2\dot\varphi=0$ gives $dt/d\varphi=\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)=\frac{15R}{16c}$.

One-turn holonomy: along the rest lines of step 2.2 the chart time changes by $\Delta t=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{15R}{16c}\,d\varphi=\frac{15\pi R}{8c}$, which is nonzero; hence the rest line starting at $\varphi=0$ returns to the same rotating label $\varphi=2\pi$ at the chart time $\Delta t>0$, and it is not closed as a curve of simultaneity. If there were a globally single-valued real function $f$ on the whole cylinder whose level sets were these rest lines, then the integral of $df$ around the closed loop $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+2\pi$ at fixed $t$ would vanish by single-valuedness, while $df$ restricted to that loop is a nowhere-zero multiple of $d\varphi$ by step 2.2, so its integral would be nonzero: a contradiction. Thus no such global synchronization time exists.

Ambient nonintegrability: for $\Omega\ne0$ the Frobenius form of the ambient congruence is $n^\flat\wedge d(n^\flat)=\gamma^2\kappa\wedge d\kappa=-2\gamma^2(\Omega/c)dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2$, which is nonzero at every point of the region $r<c/|\Omega|$; by [L2] the three-dimensional ambient rest distribution is nowhere integrable, so no local ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists there. On the cylinder the rest distribution is one-dimensional: it is locally integrable because any nowhere-zero vector field has local flow-box coordinates, and its global nontrivial holonomy is the distinct obstruction computed in step 3.1, not an instance of the ambient pointwise nonintegrability. Both the ambient congruence and the ring congruence are Born rigid by [L1].

Conclusion: steps 1.1-2.1 verify the future unit ring field; step 2.2 computes the induced cylinder metric, the rest covector and the slope $dt/d\varphi=15R/(16c)$; step 3.1 computes the exact nonzero holonomy $\Delta t=15\pi R/(8c)$ and the failure of global ring synchronization; and step 4.1 exhibits the ambient nonintegrability of the three-dimensional rest distribution. The example therefore realizes the distinction, promised by [L1], between a locally integrable one-dimensional ring distribution with nonzero global holonomy and a nowhere-integrable ambient distribution.

The computation restricts to the single ring cylinder $r=R$, $x^3=const$, with one rotating angular coordinate; the ambient field is the cited four-dimensional extension. This disposition is part of the example.
The value $\Omega R=3c/5$ keeps $c^2-\Omega^2R^2=16c^2/25>0$, so the induced cylinder metric is nondegenerate and the rest-line slope is finite. This disposition is part of the example.

Step 3.1 integrates $dt/d\varphi=15R/(16c)$ over the closed interval $[0,2\pi]$ of one positive circuit; the endpoints correspond to the same rotating label, which is exactly the non-closure statement.
The rotation rate, the radius and the ring observers are given; the holonomy is an explicit integral, and no choice principle is used. This disposition is part of the example.
Step 2.2 computes the kernel condition giving the rest-line equation, and step 3.1 integrates it to the nonzero offset $15\pi R/(8c)$.

Step 4.1 verifies the reverse obstruction direction: the ambient Frobenius form is nonzero, so the three-dimensional rest distribution is not integrable, while the ring distribution is locally integrable with the global holonomy of step 3.1.
